nameStory: The Surfbird gets its name from its preferred feeding habitat along rocky coastlines where ocean waves crash and create surf. These stocky shorebirds are almost always found right at the surf line, picking through the spray-soaked rocks for their meals of mollusks and crustaceans.
description: The Surfbird is a small, stocky shorebird that's built more like a chunky turnstone than a typical slender sandpiper. In breeding season, it shows dark streaks on a brownish head and breast with spotted white underparts, while winter birds are mostly gray and white. It has a short, thick dark bill, bright yellow legs, and a distinctive white rump with a black band at the tip that flashes when it flies.

idTips.label: White rump with black band
idTips.description: Look for the bright white rump patch crossed by a bold black stripe - this pattern is visible even from a distance when the bird flies and is unique among our sandpipers

idTips.label: Stocky build
idTips.description: Notice the chunky, robust body shape that looks more like a small turnstone than a typical thin sandpiper - it has a thick neck and broad chest

idTips.label: Short dark bill
idTips.description: The bill is notably short and thick compared to most sandpipers, appearing almost finch-like and completely dark colored

idTips.label: Bright yellow legs
idTips.description: The legs are a vivid yellow-orange color that stands out against the gray rocks where these birds feed

idTips.label: Rocky coast habitat
idTips.description: Always found on wave-splashed rocky shores rather than sandy beaches - if you're on sand, you're not looking at a Surfbird

habitat: In New England, Surfbirds are extremely rare vagrants that would only be found along rocky coastlines during migration, particularly areas with wave-washed ledges and boulder fields. They prefer the same type of rugged, surf-pounded shores where you'd find Purple Sandpipers and turnstones, avoiding sandy beaches entirely.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare migrant through New England in late spring, most likely spotted in May on rocky headlands during their northward journey to Alaska.
seasonality.summer: Not present in New England during breeding season as they nest only in the rocky tundra of Alaska and Yukon.
seasonality.fall: Best chance for a New England sighting is during fall migration from August through October when weather might blow one off course.
seasonality.winter: Does not winter in New England - continues south to rocky Pacific coasts from California to South America.

funFact: Despite being called a sandpiper, the Surfbird almost never touches sand - it's so specialized for rocky shores that it will only feed on wave-splashed boulders and ledges, making it more of a 'rockpiper' than a sandpiper!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Purple Sandpiper, which also prefers rocky coasts, but Purple Sandpiper has a longer, slightly curved bill, duller legs, and lacks the distinctive white rump with black band. Remember: Surfbird = short bill and flashy white rump with black stripe.
contextualKnowledge: The Surfbird was once placed in its own genus (Aphriza) and grouped with turnstones due to its rock-loving lifestyle, but genetic studies revealed it's actually a true sandpiper. This explains why it looks and acts so different from beach-loving sandpipers - it evolved for a completely different niche.
compareHints: Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives. While Purple Sandpiper also frequents rocks, Surfbird's shorter, thicker bill and bold rump pattern set it apart. Most other Calidris species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper are much more slender with longer bills and prefer softer substrates.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.

Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
